title: No. 9 — The Union as a Safeguard Against Domestic Faction and Insurrection (Hamilton)
paragraphs: A firm Union will be of the utmost importance to the peace and liberty of the States, as a barrier against domestic faction and insurrection. It is impossible to read the history of the petty republics of Greece and Italy without feeling horror and disgust at the constant disturbances that agitated them, and at the rapid succession of revolutions that kept them swinging endlessly between the extremes of tyranny and anarchy. The occasional periods of calm only stand as a brief contrast to the furious storms that follow. The intervals of happiness that now and then come into view are seen with a mixture of regret, born of knowing that the pleasing scenes before us will soon be overwhelmed by tempestuous waves of sedition and party rage. Brief flashes of glory may break through the gloom; but while they dazzle us with a fleeting brilliance, they also remind us to lament that the vices of government should pervert and tarnish those bright talents and exalted gifts for which the favored soils that produced them have been so justly celebrated.

But it cannot be denied that the portraits these writers sketched of republican government were too true a copy of the originals from which they were taken. If it had been impossible to devise models of a more perfect structure, the enlightened friends of liberty would have had to abandon the cause of that kind of government as indefensible. The science of politics, however, like most other sciences, has greatly improved. The effectiveness of various principles is now well understood, which were either unknown or only imperfectly known to the ancients. The orderly distribution of power into distinct departments; the introduction of legislative balances and checks; the institution of courts composed of judges who hold their offices during good behavior; the representation of the people in the legislature by deputies of their own choosing—these are wholly new discoveries, or have made their main progress toward perfection in modern times. They are means, and powerful means, by which the excellences of republican government may be retained and its imperfections lessened or avoided. To this list of features that tend to improve popular systems of civil government, I will venture to add one more—however novel it may seem to some—on a principle that has actually been used as the foundation of an objection to the new Constitution. I mean the ENLARGEMENT of the ORBIT within which such systems revolve, whether in the size of a single State or by the consolidation of several smaller States into one great Confederacy. The latter is what immediately concerns the topic at hand. It will, however, be useful to examine the principle as it applies to a single State, which I will do elsewhere.

The usefulness of a Confederacy—both for suppressing faction and guarding the internal tranquility of States, and for increasing their external force and security—is in fact not a new idea. It has been put into practice in different countries and ages, and has been endorsed by the most respected writers on the subject of politics. The opponents of the proposed plan have very busily quoted and circulated Montesquieu's observations on the necessity of a small territory for republican government. But they seem to be unaware of the views that great man expressed in another part of his work, and to have given no thought to the consequences of the principle they so readily accept.

When Montesquieu recommends a small extent for republics, the standards he had in mind were dimensions far below the limits of almost every one of these States. Neither Virginia, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, New York, North Carolina, nor Georgia can in any way be compared with the models from which he reasoned and to which the terms of his description apply. If we therefore take his ideas on this point as our test of truth, we will be driven to the choice between either taking refuge at once in the arms of monarchy, or splitting ourselves into countless little, jealous, clashing, tumultuous commonwealths—the wretched nurseries of unceasing discord and the miserable objects of universal pity or contempt. Some of the writers on the other side of the question seem to have noticed the dilemma, and have even been bold enough to hint that breaking up the larger States would be desirable. Such an infatuated policy, such a desperate expedient, might—by multiplying petty offices—suit the views of men who lack the qualifications to extend their influence beyond the narrow circles of personal intrigue. But it could never advance the greatness or happiness of the people of America.

Leaving the examination of the principle itself for another place, as already mentioned, it is enough to note here that—in the sense of the author who has been most emphatically quoted on this point—it would only call for reducing the SIZE of the more considerable MEMBERS of the Union; it would not work against having them all included in one confederate government. And that is the true question we are now interested in.

So far are Montesquieu's suggestions from opposing a general Union of the States, that he explicitly discusses a confederate republic as the means of extending the sphere of popular government and combining the advantages of monarchy with those of republicanism.

"It is very probable," he says,(1) "that mankind would have been obliged at length to live constantly under the government of a single person, had they not contrived a kind of constitution that has all the internal advantages of a republican, together with the external force of a monarchical government. I mean a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC."

"This form of government is a convention by which several smaller STATES agree to become members of a larger ONE, which they intend to form. It is a kind of assemblage of societies that constitute a new one, capable of increasing, by means of new associations, till they arrive to such a degree of power as to be able to provide for the security of the united body."
"A republic of this kind, able to withstand an external force, may support itself without any internal corruptions. The form of this society prevents all manner of inconveniences."

"If a single member should attempt to usurp the supreme authority, he could not be supposed to have an equal authority and credit in all the confederate states. Were he to have too great influence over one, this would alarm the rest. Were he to subdue a part, that which would still remain free might oppose him with forces independent of those which he had usurped and overpower him before he could be settled in his usurpation."

"Should a popular insurrection happen in one of the confederate states the others are able to quell it. Should abuses creep into one part, they are reformed by those that remain sound. The state may be destroyed on one side, and not on the other; the confederacy may be dissolved, and the confederates preserve their sovereignty."

"As this government is composed of small republics, it enjoys the internal happiness of each; and with respect to its external situation, it is possessed, by means of the association, of all the advantages of large monarchies."

I have thought it right to quote these interesting passages at length, because they contain a clear summary of the main arguments in favor of the Union, and should effectively remove the false impressions that the misapplication of other parts of his work was meant to create. They are also closely connected with the more immediate aim of this paper, which is to show the tendency of the Union to repress domestic faction and insurrection.

A distinction more subtle than accurate has been drawn between a CONFEDERACY and a CONSOLIDATION of the States. The essential feature of the first, it is said, is that its authority reaches only the members in their collective capacities, not the individuals who compose them. It is argued that the national council should have nothing to do with any object of internal administration. An exact equality of votes among the members has also been insisted on as a leading feature of a confederate government. These positions are, on the whole, arbitrary; they are supported neither by principle nor by precedent. It is true that governments of this kind have generally operated in the manner the distinction supposes to be inherent in their nature. But in most of them there have been broad exceptions to the practice, which prove—as far as example can prove anything—that there is no absolute rule on the subject. And it will be clearly shown in the course of this investigation that wherever the principle being defended has prevailed, it has been the cause of incurable disorder and weakness in government.

The definition of a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC seems simply to be "an assemblage of societies," or an association of two or more states into one state. The extent, modifications, and objects of the federal authority are mere matters of discretion. So long as the separate organization of the members is not abolished; so long as it exists, by constitutional necessity, for local purposes—though in perfect subordination to the general authority of the union—the whole would still be, in fact and in theory, an association of states, or a confederacy. The proposed Constitution, far from implying an abolition of the State governments, makes them constituent parts of the national sovereignty by allowing them a direct representation in the Senate, and leaves in their possession certain exclusive and very important portions of sovereign power. This fully corresponds, in every rational sense of the terms, with the idea of a federal government.

In the Lycian confederacy, which consisted of twenty-three CITIES or republics, the largest were entitled to THREE votes in the COMMON COUNCIL, those of the middle class to TWO, and the smallest to ONE. The COMMON COUNCIL had the appointment of all the judges and magistrates of the respective CITIES. This was certainly the most delicate kind of interference in their internal administration; for if anything seems exclusively reserved to the local jurisdictions, it is the appointment of their own officers. Yet Montesquieu, speaking of this association, says: "Were I to give a model of an excellent Confederate Republic, it would be that of Lycia." So we see that the distinctions insisted on were not in the mind of this enlightened thinker, and we are led to conclude that they are the novel refinements of a mistaken theory.
1. "Spirit of Laws," vol. i., book ix., chap. i.
